issues.legal_issue: Whether a tenant’s alterations to leased premises constitute permanent structures that support eviction depends on the circumstances of the case.
material_facts: The tenant constructed cabins and lofts after taking the premises, with pillars and stanchions sunk into the flooring and structures attached to the building.
The structures were substantial, durable, and not easily removable; the lower courts considered their nature, construction, and effect on the premises and found them permanent.
The lower courts found that the structures had been erected without the landlords’ consent.
The trial court and appellate court both ordered eviction on the ground of permanent construction.
issues.conclusion: The structures were permanent, and their erection without the landlords’ consent supported eviction under the applicable tenancy law.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 108(p) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a lessee may not erect a permanent structure without the lessor’s consent, except for agricultural purposes; section 13(1)(b) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1974 also provides a ground for eviction for permanent construction. No hard-and-fast test determines whether a structure is permanent. The court considers the structure’s nature and purpose, how it affects enjoyment of the premises, its durability, and other relevant circumstances. Surya Properties Private Ltd. v. Bimalendu Nath Sarkar, A.I.R. 1964 Calcutta 1 and A.I.R. 1965 Calcutta 408 were approved; Khureshi Ibrahim Ahmed v. Ahmed Haji Khanmahomad, A.I.R. 1965 Gujarat 152, and Ramji Virji v. Kadarbhai Esufali, A.I.R. 1973 Gujarat 110, were referred to.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_proceeding and tenant_constructed_structure_after_lease and without_landlord_consent and (substantial_structure or durable_structure or structure_affixed_to_premises)

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant from leased premises.
predicates.tenant_constructed_structure_after_lease: The tenant erected the disputed structure after taking the premises on lease.
predicates.without_landlord_consent: The tenant erected the structure without the landlord’s consent.
predicates.substantial_structure: The structure was substantial in its construction or scale.
predicates.durable_structure: The structure was intended or suited to last for a substantial period.
predicates.structure_affixed_to_premises: The structure was attached to or incorporated into the premises.

issues.definition: When a tenant facing eviction erected a structure after taking the premises without the landlord’s consent, and the structure was substantial, durable, or affixed to the premises, the tenant may be evicted for permanent construction.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court exercising supervisory jurisdiction should not overturn a lower court’s factual finding merely because it could reach a different view of the evidence.
material_facts: The trial court and appellate court both examined the evidence about the tenant’s construction and found the structures permanent.
The appellate court’s finding rested on evidence about the structures’ construction, durability, attachment, and removability, and was a possible view of the evidence.
The High Court reassessed the evidence and reversed the concurrent findings without establishing a qualifying legal or factual defect in those findings.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded the limits of its supervisory jurisdiction by reversing the lower courts’ plausible factual findings; the Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s order and restored the appellate court’s order.
issues.legal_principle: Article 227 of the Constitution confers judicial-superintendence jurisdiction, not a general appellate power to reweigh facts. Interference with a finding within the lower court’s jurisdiction is limited to cases such as perversity, legal misdirection, a factual view contrary to the preponderance of evidence, absence of material evidence, or manifest injustice. The Court relied on Satyanarayan Laxminarayan Hegde v. Mallikarjun Bhavanappa Tirumale, [1960] 1 S.C.R. 890; India Pipe Fitting Co. v. Fakruddin M.A. Baker, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 797; Ganpat Ladha v. Shashikant Vishnu Shinde, [1978] 3 S.C.R. 198; Mrs. Labhkuwar Bhagwani Shah v. Janardan Mahadeo Kalan, [1982] 3 S.C.C. 514; and Chandavarkar Sita Ratna Rao v. Ashalata S. Guram, [1986] 4 S.C.C. 447.

rule.if: supervisory_review_of_lower_court_facts and factual_finding_within_lower_court_jurisdiction and plausible_factual_finding and not finding_perverse and not legal_misdirection and not contrary_to_preponderance_of_evidence and not unsupported_by_material_evidence and not manifest_injustice

predicates.supervisory_review_of_lower_court_facts: A party sought supervisory review of factual findings made by a lower court or tribunal.
predicates.factual_finding_within_lower_court_juris: The lower court made the finding on a matter within its jurisdiction.
predicates.plausible_factual_finding: The finding was a possible view based on the evidence considered by the lower court.
predicates.finding_perverse: The finding was one that no reasonable person properly instructed in law could have reached.
predicates.legal_misdirection: The lower court reached its finding after misdirecting itself on the law.
predicates.contrary_to_preponderance_of_evidence: The factual view was taken in the face of the preponderance of the evidence.
predicates.unsupported_by_material_evidence: The finding was not based on material evidence.
predicates.manifest_injustice: The finding resulted in manifest injustice.

issues.definition: When supervisory review concerns a plausible factual finding within the lower court’s jurisdiction and none of the stated defects is present, the High Court must not interfere with that finding.
